articles.title: California election officials frustrated, rattled by DOJ demand to sequester 'noncitizen' ballots
articles.description: California election officials frustrated, rattled by DOJ demand to sequester 'noncitizen' ballots AP News California leader calls attack on alleged noncitizen voting ‘weaponizing the law’ The Guardian DOJ orders some California counties to verify ballots in 48 hours AP News Justice Dept. Demands That California Counties Help Identify Noncitizen Voters The New York Times UPDATED Nevada County joins a growing list of c
articles.content: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Local election officials across California are confused and frustrated after receiving letters from President Donald Trump’s Justice Department demanding that county registrars sequester ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections. The letters, which were sent on Friday, ask for sensitive information, including Social Security numbers, on roughly 20,000 voters. It is illegal for noncitizens to register to vote or cast a ballot. The administration has insisted that immigrants voting is a major problem nationwide, when in fact it is quite rare, as even its own investigations have shown. “All of this is simply meant to raise huge doubts about the integrity of this election,” said John Tuteur, the registrar of voters for Napa County in California’s wine country. Tuteur and other election officials who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday said they have already started to count ballots that have trickled in from the state’s 23 million registered voters. “We’re not changing anything we’re doing. We’re proceeding with the election,” he said. The federal government set a 48-hour deadline to provide information, and it warned that legal action could be taken against any official who knowingly counted a noncitizen’s vote. However, the California attorney general’s office said the letters contained errors. For example, Mendocino County officials received a list of people who were not residents there, according to the state’s court filing. The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between Democratic-dominated California and Trump’s Department of Justice ahead of the midterms. The federal government sued on Oct. 15, roughly three weeks before elections, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens. A panel of 9th Circuit appeals court judges will hear arguments on Sunday about whether California can be compelled to comply with the federal government’s demands. Tuteur said that two uniformed Department of Homeland Security officers delivered a letter to his office late on Friday afternoon. The letter included the names of 42 people who the federal government accused of being noncitizens illegally registered to vote. There are roughly 86,000 people registered to vote across the county of over 130,000 people, Tuteur said. Approximately 11,000 people had already cast a mail-in ballot as of Friday. In larger counties like Los Angeles, that number has already reached over 331,000 counted mail-in votes. He said his employees and his relatives were worried about what could come next. “My family’s upset, worried about what’s going to happen to me,” he said. The letter sent to Clerk-Recorder Kim Grady’s office in rural Amador County listed four people allegedly illegally registered to vote in the county. Grady was waiting on more guidance from the state about what she should do, and she wasn’t sure if she would get any clarity before the deadline. Department of Justice spokeswoman Kiersten Pels emphasized in a statement on Saturday that the department is explicitly “not requesting a purge, cancellation of registrations, or any programmatic action.” Instead, Pels wrote, federal officials are asking for collaboration to “ensure the most secure election in California history.” The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities on Monday, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said that the clerks who didn’t comply with the government’s demands could face prosecution as well. “The letters speak for themselves. Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy,” Essayli said in a statement. Noncitizen voting is very rare. For example, earlier this month Attorney General Todd Blanche announced federal charges against 10 people in Minnesota alleged to have voted illegally over the last three elections, a period in which more than 8 million ballots were cast in the state. But Essayli said on Monday that even a small number of illegal voters could “dilute” the vote and undermine confidence in elections. Some election officials who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday have questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s list of 20,000 voters. “I expect this accusation to fall apart like we saw recently in Nevada,” Kristin B. Connelly, the Contra Costa County clerk-recorder and registrar of voters said, referring to remarks Trump made in July, when he claimed the neighboring state had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its rolls. After his administration was asked to identify them, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. Officials in Los Angeles County, who are named as defendants in the federal lawsuit, have echoed Connelly’s concerns about the federal government’s data. A preliminary analysis of 200 names from the statewide list of 20,000 found that over 40% had canceled registrations, according to a court filing from county officials on Wednesday. More than 70% of that sample had no voting history whatsoever, and nearly 4 in 10 were born in the United States.

articles.title: Obama rallies rapturous Michigan crowd for El-Sayed: ‘He’ll finish the job we started’
articles.content: Former president speaks to crowd of thousands in support of Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate and Democratic ticket Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan. Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”. The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”. He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said. The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP. The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations. Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?” On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said. He even took a jab at Trump’s attempts to renovate the White House. “He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of the many renovations in Washington, including the White House ballroom and the Rose Garden. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure. El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month. Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up. Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.” “We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said. A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe. Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker. Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan’s first Black governor. Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed “didn’t like some things you did as president”. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” “We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society,” Obama said, “and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.”

articles.title: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida
articles.description: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida AP News Trump, Who Once Called Early Voting ‘Ridiculous,’ Casts a Midterm Ballot The New York Times President Trump, first lady vote early in person in Florida CBS News Trump casts his midterm election ballot early in Florida CNBC Trump pushes mail ballots amid DOJ election lawsuits Salon.com
articles.content: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally. Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the president spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has been criticized in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots. Asked if he voted the party line, Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.” Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12. Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.” Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine. In Florida, Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. He has also campaigned for Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.

articles.content: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies, as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania. The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions. The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment. [Media: https://youtu.be/zvfHKeqHFNw]

A teenager starved to death months after being detained. Her mom’s taking police to court
articles.content: In the 18 days Runa spent in a police cell in Japan, she wrote about how much she yearned to come home. The teenager missed her mother’s cooking, her hugs, and their small, ordinary rituals of life together – reading, shopping, and singing. “Please, I beg you. I want to see my mom,” she scribbled in a notepad given to her during her detention, seen by CNN. Runa’s incarceration – and death months after her release – is now the subject of a lawsuit brought by her mother against Hyogo Prefectural Police alleging unlawful arrest and detention. Proceedings opened this week in a case that’s shone a spotlight on Japan’s treatment of juvenile suspects. “I feel so sorry for Runa that I failed to protect her myself,” Runa’s mother Yoko told CNN through tears and staggered breaths, using an alias for privacy reasons. CNN has withheld Runa’s full name at her mother’s request, for the same reason. Yoko said Japanese police held the 16-year-old for 18 days last year on suspicion of an assault at the care home she runs for people with special needs. Police declined to comment or share details of the complaint, and CNN has been unable to independently verify the allegations. Yoko said her daughter simply tried to prevent an agitated resident from biting others by putting her hand around the person’s chin. Runa denied the allegation and was never charged. During her incarceration, Runa stopped eating and after her release, she was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. Her weight continued to drop, and she died five months later, weighing about 20 kilograms — the average weight of a 6-year-old girl. Her single mother is seeking 109 million yen ($700,000) in damages, alleging unlawful arrest and detention, which she said led to Runa’s death. “I want the police and prosecutors to reflect on their duty to care for people and protect citizens, and to tell the truth in court,” she said. The rules around juveniles in custody Japan has a reputation for “hostage justice,” a term referring to the detention of suspects without charge for far longer than the law in other countries would allow, often for days, if not weeks. But the country also has strict rules governing how minors should be treated during a criminal investigation. Under Japan’s Juvenile Law, minors should only be incarcerated when it’s “unavoidable.” However, defense attorney Megumi Wada said the meaning of “unavoidable” had never been clearly defined, and was open to interpretation by authorities. More than 6,000 suspects under the age of 20 were detained in 2024 – and of those, 4,000 were held for more than 15 days, according to government statistics. The decision to deny Runa access to her mother, and detain her for more than a fortnight, has baffled lawyers, raising questions about whether measures to protect minors in custody are working. Mikio Uehara, a public prosecutor turned defense attorney, said Runa’s death was “extremely tragic.” “I have strong doubts as to whether detention was truly necessary,” he added. When asked for the reasons behind Runa’s detention, the Hyogo Prefectural Police said it would not “comment on the details of individual cases.” “This matter is currently the subject of a pending lawsuit for state compensation, and the prefecture’s position will be made clear in court,” a spokesperson said. Japan’s Ministry of Justice has repeatedly rejected allegations of “hostage justice,” saying that it gives due consideration to the rights of people accused of wrongdoing. A life upended The family runs a care home in Hyogo prefecture, located in the northwest of Osaka, Japan’s second-biggest city. Growing up around people who needed extra care, Runa was a “cheerful girl” who aspired to take over the family care home one day, her mother said. “Although her life was short, only 16 years, she lived every single day without ever forgetting compassion and care for others,” said Yoko. But the arrest of Runa on June 17 last year – four months after the alleged assault – upended everything. Police detained Runa at the care home and took her away before her mother, who had rushed back to the facility upon hearing the news, had a chance to see her, Yoko recalled. For the next 18 days, Yoko was barred from visiting Runa due to a ban sought by the prosecutors – and granted by a court – over concerns that she, as the owner of the facility, could tamper with the evidence. Through Runa’s lawyer, she began to learn that her daughter wasn’t eating properly. But she was never informed of the full extent as authorities rejected her requests for Runa’s meal records, she said. The night before her release, the teenager collapsed and was rushed to the hospital, she said. The next morning, Yoko was shocked by what she saw. “She had become skin and bones and came out screaming and crying,” Yoko recalled. “Her stride was so feeble it took everything she had just to walk 10 meters, not even 5 meters,” she said, adding that they had to carry her to the car. An anxious child Apart from her scribbled notes, scant details are available about Runa’s experience in detention, according to her lawyer Yoshihiro Mukai. “When we met her, she was overwhelmed with anxiety, repeatedly asking what would become of her,” Mukai told CNN, of their meetings during her detention. Japan has facilities – known as Shonen Kanbetsu Sho – dedicated to temporarily housing juvenile suspects. But defense lawyer Wada said they were seldom used when the detention was shorter than two weeks, leaving minors to face similar conditions to their adult counterparts. It’s not clear why Runa wasn’t moved to a juvenile facility after the first two weeks in custody. Wada also raised another peculiarity in Runa’s case. “I have never seen cases where the parents couldn’t see the suspects,” she said. A separate police guideline requires investigators to do their best to accommodate juvenile suspects’ requests for the company of an appropriate adult, such as a parent, even during interrogation. But the right is not absolute, said Tomonobu Ishida, a law professor at Meiji University in Tokyo. “They are essentially internal rules or administrative guidelines for the police, and therefore do not have the legally binding force,” Ishida said. “However, even assuming that there was a genuine risk of destruction of evidence, I personally have some difficulty seeing how such a relatively long period of detention could be considered proportionate, given the relatively minor nature of the alleged conduct and the fact that she was a juvenile,” Ishida said. Calls for change After Runa’s release early last July, she became suspicious of adults, including the doctors and nurses who came to treat her, Yoko said. Yoko said they tried to feed her food that might revive her appetite – from ice cream to nuts – but “everything just passed right through her system.” Runa’s distrust in the system complicated rescue efforts as she refused to be taken to hospital. Psychiatrist Mai Uchida said it’s crucial not to mistake teenagers for a “smaller version of adults,” saying their emotional and cognitive control is still developing, which causes them to experience and process stress very differently. Runa’s death was attributed to malnutrition due to an eating disorder. Loss of appetite is common following traumatic events, she said, adding that it cannot be reversed simply by encouraging the person to eat more. “It is certainly possible that PTSD could cause functional difficulties in the (gastrointestinal) system, as well as making a difference in the appetite and causing significant amount of weight loss and that would connect to death,” said Uchida, an associate psychiatry professor at Harvard Medical School. Human rights groups have long warned of the undue stress suspects in Japan are subject to during detention, ranging from aggressive questioning tactics to the lack of access to lawyers. Some legal experts said prolonged detention occurs far too often, regardless of the suspect’s age. In 2024, about 65% of the 85,040 adults detained in Japan spent more than 15 days in police custody, according to government statistics. “I completely fail to understand how such a practice is allowed to pass, and this broader reality urgently needs reform as well,” said lawyer Uehara. Yoko hopes her bid to seek justice on her daughter’s behalf could play a role in driving change. “Winning this lawsuit would mean that, even if Runa is no longer physically here, it will serve as proof that she lived and left a legacy behind to reform this justice system.”
